chunks.title: Eyelid glands: who's who
chunks.tldr: Lid margin glands: Meibomian (in the tarsus), Zeis (oil, at lashes), Moll (sweat, at lashes).
points: Meibomian glands = modified oil glands in the tarsal plate. 20–30 openings per lid. They make the oily outer layer of the tear film.
Zeis glands = small oil glands attached to lash follicles.
Moll glands = modified apocrine sweat glands at the lash line. More of them in the lower lid.
Eccrine sweat glands = all over the lid skin, not just the margin.
Epidermis layers from the top: keratin → granular → prickle (spinosum) → basal.
chunks.hook: Meibomian = Main oil factory. Zeis = oil at the lashes (Z sounds like 'seize the lash'). Moll = moist (sweat).

cards.q: Which lid gland is a modified apocrine sweat gland?
Meibomian glands make which tear layer?

chunks.title: Skin words you need to know
chunks.tldr: Flat = macule. Raised <1 cm = papule. Raised >1 cm = nodule/plaque. Fluid: vesicle (<0.5 cm) or bulla (>0.5 cm).
points: Macule: flat colour change, <1 cm. Papule: solid bump, <1 cm. Pustule: pus bump.
Nodule: solid lump >1 cm. Plaque: flat-topped raised area >1 cm.
Hyperkeratosis = thick keratin → looks scaly.
Acanthosis = thick prickle-cell layer.
Parakeratosis = nuclei left in the keratin layer. Dyskeratosis = keratin made in the wrong place.
Carcinoma in situ (Bowen) = dysplasia through the full thickness of the epidermis, but not invading yet.
Benign-looking lesion: no ulcer, even colour, slow, regular edge, lid margin and lashes left intact.
chunks.hook: Lashes lost = worry. Benign things usually leave the lid margin alone.

cards.q: Fluid blister 0.8 cm: vesicle or bulla?
Retained nuclei in the keratin layer is called?

chunks.title: Chalazion
chunks.tldr: A chalazion is a sterile blocked meibomian gland that forms a lipogranuloma. A recurrent one needs a biopsy.
points: Painless, slowly growing lump in the tarsal plate.
If it gets infected it's called an internal hordeolum.
Linked with blepharitis and rosacea (multiple/recurrent). Drug cause: bortezomib (myeloma drug).
About 1/3 go away on their own → warm compresses first.
Steroid injection (triamcinolone) works about as well as surgery (~80% after one shot). Good near the punctum. Risks: skin depigmentation, fat atrophy, and rarely retinal artery occlusion.
Incision & curettage: clamp, cut vertically through the tarsus on the inside, scrape it out. No stitches.
Antibiotics only if truly infected. Recurrent + rosacea → oral tetracycline.
chunks.hook: Same chalazion keeps coming back? Think sebaceous gland carcinoma in disguise → biopsy.
pearls: Chalazion fat is extracellular (lipogranuloma). Xanthelasma fat is intracellular (foam cells).

cards.q: Elderly woman with a third recurrence of the same upper-lid 'chalazion'. Next step?
cards.a: Biopsy to rule out sebaceous gland carcinoma.

cards.q: Which myeloma drug causes chalazia?

chunks.title: Other eyelid cysts
chunks.tldr: Moll = see-through (clear fluid). Zeis = not see-through (oily). Dermoid = lateral brow.
points: Cyst of Zeis: small, opaque, on the front lid margin.
Cyst of Moll (apocrine hidrocystoma): round, translucent, fluid-filled, on the lid margin.
Eccrine hidrocystoma: like Moll, but near (not on) the margin, medially or laterally.
Milia: tiny white bumps in crops (trapped keratin).
Epidermal inclusion cyst: after trauma or surgery, firm and full of keratin.
Dermoid cyst: from birth, stuck to bone at the lateral end of the brow.
Comedones: blackheads (open) or whiteheads (closed).

cards.q: Translucent cyst on the lid margin?
Child with a firm lump at the lateral brow, fixed to bone?

chunks.title: Xanthelasma
chunks.tldr: Yellow plaques on the medial lids. About 1/3 have high lipids, so check them.
points: Middle-aged and older people, often both sides, often several.
Fat is inside cells: lipid-laden foam cells in the dermis.
May come with corneal arcus if lipids are high.
Treatment is cosmetic: excision, microdissection, TCA peel, laser, cryo.
Comes back in up to 50%, especially with high cholesterol.

cards.q: Xanthelasma: what proportion have hyperlipidaemia?

chunks.title: Benign skin growths
chunks.tldr: Skin tag = papilloma. Stuck-on greasy brown = seborrhoeic keratosis. Scaly sun spot = actinic keratosis, which can turn into SCC.
points: Squamous papilloma: very common. Skin tag (pedunculated), broad-based, or thread-like. Some are from HPV. Snip it off.
Seborrhoeic keratosis (basal cell papilloma): brown, greasy, warty, 'stuck-on' look, elderly. Can look like pigmented BCC or melanoma.
Actinic keratosis: scaly plaque on sun-damaged skin in fair elderly people. Pre-malignant → SCC. Biopsy, then excise or freeze.
Any of these can grow a cutaneous horn. Cut deep: there may be SCC underneath.

cards.q: Which benign lesion has a 'stuck-on' appearance?
Which can transform into SCC: seborrhoeic or actinic keratosis?

chunks.title: Moles (naevi) & freckles
chunks.tldr: Naevi change with age: junctional (young, flat) → compound (raised) → intradermal (old, pale, no cancer risk).
points: Freckle: 1–5 mm brown macule, more melanin but a normal number of melanocytes.
Junctional naevus: young person, flat, evenly brown. Cells sit at the epidermis–dermis junction. Low risk.
Compound naevus: middle age, raised. Cells at the junction and in the dermis. Low risk.
Intradermal naevus: most common, older people, raised, pale, may have lashes growing from it. No malignant potential.
Split ('kissing') naevus: congenital, on both upper and lower lid.
Giant congenital naevus: up to 15% become malignant.
Atypical mole syndrome → higher risk of skin, conjunctival and uveal melanoma.
If melanoma is suspected → excise with a 3 mm margin.
chunks.hook: Moles sink with age: junction → both → dermis only.

cards.q: Which acquired naevus type has no malignant potential?
What is a 'kissing' naevus?
cards.a: A congenital split naevus across the upper and lower lid.

chunks.title: Kids' lumps: haemangioma & pilomatricoma
chunks.tldr: Strawberry red lump in a baby = capillary haemangioma → topical beta-blocker. Hard purple nodule in a kid = pilomatricoma.
points: Capillary haemangioma: one of the commonest infant tumours, 3× more in girls. Appears soon after birth, usually upper lid.
Bright red (deeper = purplish), blanches when pressed, swells when crying.
Can cause ptosis → risk of amblyopia. Can extend into the orbit.
Many skin lesions → think about internal (visceral) haemangiomas.
Treat with a topical beta-blocker (more in Ch 4).
Pilomatricoma: from hair-bulb cells, kids and young adults (more in females). Hard (calcified), mobile, purplish nodule. Excise.
Syringoma: small, multiple papules from eccrine sweat glands.

cards.q: Treatment of a small eyelid capillary haemangioma?
Hard, calcified, mobile nodule in a child's lid?

chunks.title: Port-wine stain & Sturge–Weber
chunks.tldr: Port-wine stain = flat pink patch that doesn't blanch, along a trigeminal branch. Screen for glaucoma from infancy.
points: Congenital malformation of small skin vessels (not a tumour).
One side of the face. Gets darker and lumpier with age, with soft-tissue overgrowth.
About 10% have eye or brain involvement.
Sturge–Weber: port-wine stain + leptomeningeal haemangioma (→ seizures, hemiparesis, hemianopia) + eye problems.
Eye problems: same-side glaucoma, episcleral haemangioma, iris heterochromia, diffuse choroidal haemangioma.
Treatment: pulsed-dye laser (best done early).
Pyogenic granuloma: fast-growing red lump that bleeds easily, after surgery or trauma. Excise.
Plexiform neurofibroma: S-shaped upper lid = NF1.
pearls: S-shaped upper lid in a child → plexiform neurofibroma → NF1.

cards.q: Port-wine stain on the face. What eye condition must you screen for?
S-shaped upper lid deformity?

chunks.title: Syndromes that cause lid cancers in young people
chunks.tldr: Lid cancer in a young patient → think of a predisposing syndrome.
points: Xeroderma pigmentosum (AR): sunlight destroys the skin → many BCCs, SCCs, melanomas. Photophobia. 'Bird-like' face.
Gorlin–Goltz (AD): many small BCCs from the teens, plus bone/face problems and medulloblastoma.
Muir–Torre (AD): sebaceous carcinoma, BCC, keratoacanthoma + colon/GU cancers.
Bazex: multiple BCCs (X-linked dominant form) or a sign of upper GI/respiratory cancer.
Others: immunosuppression, past retinoblastoma, albinism.

cards.q: Sebaceous carcinoma + colorectal cancer?
Multiple BCCs in a teenager, AD inheritance?

chunks.title: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)
chunks.tldr: BCC = 90% of lid cancers. Lower lid most common. Grows locally, doesn't spread. Medial canthus ones are the worst.
points: Commonest human cancer. Risks: fair skin, sun, can't tan.
Where: lower lid → medial canthus → upper lid → lateral canthus.
Nodular: shiny, pearly nodule with tiny vessels on top.
Nodulo-ulcerative ('rodent ulcer'): central ulcer, rolled pearly edges, telangiectasia.
Sclerosing (morphoeic): flat, hard, hidden edges. Much bigger than it looks. Mimics one-sided chronic blepharitis.
Histology: palisading basal cells at the edge of tumour lobules.
Medial canthus BCC → invades orbit and sinuses, recurs most. Recurrent BCC is more aggressive.
chunks.hook: BCC = Big Common but Calm (doesn't metastasise). Pearls and rolled edges.
pearls: Unilateral 'blepharitis' that won't settle → think sclerosing BCC or sebaceous carcinoma.

cards.q: Commonest malignant eyelid tumour, and the commonest site?
Which BCC location carries the highest recurrence and orbital invasion risk?

chunks.title: SCC & keratoacanthoma
chunks.tldr: SCC is rarer but nastier than BCC: ~20% spread to lymph nodes, plus perineural spread. Keratoacanthoma grows fast, then shrinks.
points: SCC = 5–10% of lid cancers. Lower lid and lid margin.
Can come from actinic keratosis or Bowen disease. Higher risk with immunosuppression (AIDS, transplant) and XP.
Compared with BCC: grows faster, more keratin/scale, usually no pearly edge or surface vessels.
Check the regional lymph nodes. Can creep along nerves into the skull.
Histology: keratin pearls, eosinophilic atypical cells.
Keratoacanthoma: pink dome, doubles in weeks, stops, then goes away over a year leaving a keratin-filled crater and a scar. Excise anyway (3 mm margin or Mohs).
Keratoacanthoma or cutaneous horn may hide invasive SCC deeper down.

cards.q: Roughly what % of eyelid SCCs spread to regional lymph nodes?
Lesion that doubles in size in weeks then involutes leaving a crater?

chunks.title: Sebaceous gland carcinoma: the great mimic
chunks.tldr: SGC loves the upper lid, elderly women, and pretends to be a chalazion or blepharitis.
points: Usually from meibomian glands (sometimes Zeis). That's why it's on the upper lid, which has more meibomian glands.
Yellowish material in a lid lump = strongly suggests SGC.
Nodular: hard lump in the upper tarsus → looks like a chalazion.
Spreading: diffuse lid-margin thickening, lash loss → looks like blepharitis.
Pagetoid spread: tumour creeps inside the epithelium (e.g. onto the conjunctiva).
Mortality 5–10%. Worse with: upper lid, size ≥10 mm, symptoms >6 months.
Histology: pale, foamy, vacuolated cells.
chunks.hook: BCC and SCC go low (lower lid). SGC goes up (upper lid).

cards.q: Which lid cancer is more common on the upper lid?
Name 3 bad prognostic features of SGC.
cards.a: Upper lid, size ≥10 mm, symptoms >6 months.

chunks.title: Melanoma, Merkel cell & Kaposi
chunks.tldr: Half of lid melanomas have no pigment. Merkel cell = violet nodule, half have spread already. Kaposi = AIDS.
points: Melanoma warning signs: new or changing, irregular edge, asymmetric, many colours, >6 mm.
Lentigo maligna (Hutchinson freckle) = melanoma in situ. Slowly spreading flat brown patch in old sun-damaged skin. A lump appearing in it = invasion.
Superficial spreading melanoma = irregular plaque. Nodular melanoma = blue-black nodule. Treat with wide excision ± nodes.
Merkel cell carcinoma: fast, very malignant. Violet nodule, intact skin, upper lid. 50% have metastasised at diagnosis.
Kaposi sarcoma: red-violet lesion in HIV/AIDS. May be the first sign of HIV. Radiotherapy or excision + treat HIV.
chunks.hook: Melanoma ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving.

cards.q: What fraction of eyelid melanomas are non-pigmented?
Violaceous upper lid nodule with intact skin, elderly patient, often already metastatic?

chunks.title: Treating lid cancers: cut, check, rebuild
chunks.tldr: Cut it out, prove the margins are clear, then rebuild. Mohs is best for tumours with fuzzy edges.
points: Small BCC: excise with a 2–4 mm margin. SCC, SGC and melanoma need wider margins.
Frozen section: check the margins during surgery, rebuild the same day.
Mohs: remove layer by layer, mapping until clear. Best for sclerosing BCC, SCC, recurrences, canthal tumours.
Rebuild both layers: front (skin + muscle) and back (tarsus + conjunctiva). At least one needs its own blood supply.
<1/3 of the lid → direct closure (± lateral cantholysis). Up to 1/2 → Tenzel semicircular flap. >1/2 → Hughes flap (upper-lid tarsoconjunctival flap, cut free after 4–6 weeks) or grafts.
Laissez-faire: leave the wound to heal by itself. Works surprisingly well.
Radiotherapy: for people who can't have surgery, or for Kaposi. Avoid at the medial canthus (scars the tear ducts) and upper lid (keratinises the conjunctiva → sore cornea).
chunks.hook: Thirds rule: ⅓ close it, ½ flap it (Tenzel), more = Hughes.

cards.q: Lower-lid defect of 60% after BCC excision: which reconstruction?
cards.a: Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap (posterior lamella) + skin graft/flap.

cards.q: Best excision technique for sclerosing BCC?

chunks.title: Misdirected lashes: trichiasis vs distichiasis
chunks.tldr: Trichiasis = lashes from the normal spot, pointing the wrong way. Distichiasis = an extra row growing from the meibomian openings.
points: Lid margin, front to back: lashes → grey line → meibomian openings → mucocutaneous junction → conjunctiva.
Trichiasis: after blepharitis, zoster, injury, or chalazion surgery.
Marginal entropion: very common, often missed. The back of the lid scars and rolls a row of lashes inward. The mucocutaneous junction moves forward.
Congenital distichiasis: AD. Often with lymphoedema of the legs (lymphoedema–distichiasis). Soft lashes, symptoms start around age 5.
Acquired distichiasis: meibomian glands turn into lash follicles after severe inflammation: chemical burn, SJS, OCP. Stubby, pale, scratchy lashes.
Symptoms: scratchy eye worse on blinking, PEEs, and later ulcers and pannus.

cards.q: Extra lash row + swollen legs since childhood?
Name 3 causes of acquired distichiasis.
cards.a: Chemical injury, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid.

chunks.title: Fixing bad lashes + other lash problems
chunks.tldr: A few lashes → epilate, electrolysis or laser. Lots of lashes → surgery or cryo.
points: Epilation: quick, but they always grow back within weeks.
Electrolysis / hyfrecation or laser (aimed down the follicle): for a few lashes. Often needs repeating.
Tarsal fracture: for marginal entropion. Cut across the tarsus from inside, then add everting sutures.
Pentagon resection: for a small clump of bad lashes.
Cryotherapy (−20 °C, double freeze-thaw): for many lashes, but lots of side effects.
Trichomegaly (long lashes): prostaglandin drops, phenytoin, ciclosporin, HIV, hypothyroidism.
Madarosis (lash loss): blepharitis, infiltrating tumour, burns, radiotherapy, alopecia, hypothyroidism, SLE, leprosy, trichotillomania.
Poliosis (white lashes): blepharitis, sympathetic ophthalmia, VKH, Waardenburg, vitiligo.

cards.q: Glaucoma drop that makes lashes long?
Poliosis + bilateral granulomatous uveitis + hearing loss?

chunks.title: Allergic & immune lid swelling
chunks.tldr: Sudden puffy lids on both sides = allergic oedema. Scaly itchy lids after new drops = contact dermatitis (type IV).
points: Acute allergic oedema: pollen or insect bite. Both lids boggy, ± chemosis. Antihistamine if needed.
Contact dermatitis: eye drops, cosmetics, metals. Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity. Scaly, tight, fissured skin. Stop the cause, cold compresses.
Atopic dermatitis: eczema + asthma + hay fever. Thick, cracked lids. Linked to staph blepharitis, VKC/AKC, keratoconus, cataract, RD.
Atopics get worse herpes → eczema herpeticum.
Dermatomyositis: heliotrope (purple) lid rash + muscle weakness. In adults, look for a hidden cancer (ovary, breast, lung).
chunks.hook: Purple lids + weak muscles = dermatomyositis → look for cancer in adults.

cards.q: Contact dermatitis is which hypersensitivity type?
Heliotrope rash on the lids?

chunks.title: Bacterial lid infections
chunks.tldr: Stye = staph abscess of a lash follicle/Zeis. Honey crusts = impetigo. Black skin = necrotizing fasciitis (emergency!).
points: External hordeolum (stye): tender lump on the lid margin pointing out through the skin, a lash at its tip. Warm compress, pull the lash, ± antibiotic.
Internal hordeolum = infected meibomian gland (see chalazion).
Impetigo: Staph aureus or Strep pyogenes, kids, blisters with golden crusts. Very contagious. Keep away from newborns.
Erysipelas: Strep pyogenes, red plaque with a sharp raised edge.
Necrotizing fasciitis: Strep pyogenes. Redness → big blisters → black necrosis. Needs urgent debridement and IV antibiotics, or the patient may die.
chunks.hook: Impetigo = honey-coloured crusts. Erysipelas = edge you can feel.

cards.q: Organism of a stye?
Golden-yellow crusts around a child's eye?

chunks.title: Viral lid infections
chunks.tldr: One-sided follicular conjunctivitis that won't settle? Look for a molluscum on the lid margin.
points: Molluscum contagiosum: poxvirus (DNA), kids aged 2–4. Pale, waxy, umbilicated (central dimple) nodules.
A lid-margin molluscum sheds virus into the tears → chronic follicular conjunctivitis on the same side.
Lots of mollusca → think immunosuppression (HIV).
Histology: Henderson–Patterson inclusion bodies.
Treatment: often goes away on its own. Otherwise shave, curette, or freeze it.
Herpes simplex: tingling, then clustered vesicles. Not as neatly one-sided as zoster. Can cause dendritic ulcers. Treat with aciclovir cream or oral antivirals.
HZO: sharp one-sided dermatome rash (details in Ch 7).

cards.q: Chronic unilateral follicular conjunctivitis not responding to antibiotics. What do you look for?
cards.a: Molluscum contagiosum on the lid margin.

cards.q: Inclusion bodies of molluscum?

chunks.title: Blepharitis: the three types
chunks.tldr: Anterior (lash base: staph or seborrhoeic) vs posterior (meibomian gland dysfunction). Usually a mix, usually both eyes.
points: Symptoms: burning, gritty, crusty, red lid margins, worse in the morning. Symptoms often don't match the signs.
Staphylococcal: hard scales, collarettes around lashes, lash loss, notching, styes. Linked to atopic dermatitis. Can cause marginal keratitis and phlyctens.
Seborrhoeic: greasy, soft scales, sticky lashes. Linked to seborrhoeic dermatitis (scalp, nose folds).
Posterior (MGD): capped or plugged meibomian openings, toothpaste-like secretions, foamy tear film. Linked to acne rosacea.
Demodex mites: cylindrical dandruff (collarettes). Rotate the lash at the slit lamp to see them. Longus → anterior, brevis → posterior.

cards.q: Foamy tear film and toothpaste-like meibum: which blepharitis?
Cylindrical collarettes at lash bases suggest which organism?

chunks.title: Treating blepharitis
chunks.tldr: No cure, just control: warm compress + lid scrub every day, plus antibiotics or a short steroid when it flares.
points: Warm compress for a few minutes → scrub the lid margin (diluted baby shampoo or bicarbonate) → massage the meibomian glands.
Topical antibiotic ointment (fusidic acid, chloramphenicol, azithromycin) for anterior folliculitis.
Oral doxycycline (better for posterior) or azithromycin (better for anterior).
No tetracyclines under 12, or in pregnancy or breastfeeding (they stain teeth and bone). Use erythromycin instead.
Short mild steroid (FML, loteprednol) for bad inflammation.
Plus: tear substitutes, omega-3, tea tree oil for Demodex, ciclosporin, IPL, LipiFlow.

cards.q: Why avoid doxycycline in an 8-year-old with blepharitis?
cards.a: It deposits in growing teeth and bone. Use erythromycin instead.

cards.q: Tea tree oil targets which organism?

chunks.title: Lice, ticks, angular & childhood blepharitis
chunks.tldr: Crab lice on the lashes (6 legs) → pull them off + delouse everyone. Angular blepharitis = Moraxella.
points: Phthiriasis palpebrarum: pubic louse on the lashes, with nits (pearly eggs) stuck at the lash base. Remove with forceps, use petroleum jelly, and treat family, clothes and bedding.
Lice have 6 legs, ticks have 8.
Ticks: remove early and close to the skin (Lyme needs ≥36 h attached). Pyrethrin/permethrin first, then forceps.
Angular blepharitis: red, cracked skin at the canthi. Moraxella lacunata or Staph. Chloramphenicol or erythromycin.
Childhood blepharokeratoconjunctivitis: around age 6, recurrent styes/chalazia, phlyctens, corneal haze, photophobia (often misdiagnosed as allergy). Lid hygiene, low-dose steroid, oral erythromycin.

cards.q: Organism of angular blepharitis?
Lice on eyelashes are usually which species?

chunks.title: Ptosis: 4 causes + fake ptosis
chunks.tldr: Ptosis causes: Neurogenic, Myogenic, Aponeurotic, Mechanical. First rule out pseudoptosis.
points: Neurogenic: 3rd nerve palsy, Horner.
Myogenic: myasthenia, myotonic dystrophy, CPEO.
Aponeurotic (involutional): stretched levator tendon. Old age, contact lenses.
Mechanical: heavy mass or scarring.

Pseudoptosis (looks droopy but isn't): no globe support (artificial eye, phthisis, enophthalmos), retraction of the other lid, hypotropia on the same side (the lid follows the eye down), brow ptosis, dermatochalasis.
Hypotropia trick: cover the good eye. If the 'ptosis' goes away, it was pseudoptosis.

cards.q: Ptosis disappears when you cover the normal eye. Why?
cards.a: Pseudoptosis from ipsilateral hypotropia: the eye takes up fixation and the lid follows it up.

cards.q: Name 2 myogenic causes of acquired ptosis.

chunks.title: Measuring ptosis (the numbers)
chunks.tldr: Key numbers: MRD1 4–5 mm, levator function ≥15 mm normal, ≤4 mm poor.
points: MRD (margin–reflex distance): upper lid edge to the corneal light reflex. Normal 4–5 mm.
Palpebral fissure: men 7–10 mm, women 8–12 mm. Upper lid normally covers the top 2 mm of cornea.
Ptosis grade: mild ≤2 mm, moderate 3 mm, severe ≥4 mm.
Levator function: hold the brow still (block frontalis), measure lid travel from looking down to looking up. Normal ≥15, good 12–14, fair 5–11, poor ≤4 mm.
Lid crease: women ~10 mm, men ~8 mm. No crease → poor levator (congenital). High crease → aponeurotic.
Always check: pupils (Horner, 3rd nerve), fatigue (look up for 30–60 s → myasthenia; Cogan lid twitch), eye movements, jaw-wink, Bell phenomenon, tear film.
Lift the droopy lid: if the other lid drops → Hering's law. Warn the patient the other side may drop after surgery.
chunks.hook: High crease = old tendon (aponeurotic). No crease = weak muscle (congenital).

cards.q: Normal MRD1?
Levator function of 3 mm is graded as?
Lid overshoot on looking back up from downgaze?

chunks.title: Congenital ptosis & jaw-winking
chunks.tldr: Congenital ptosis: poor levator, no crease, and the lid stays higher on downgaze. Marcus Gunn = the lid jumps up when chewing.
points: Simple congenital ptosis: the levator doesn't relax, so on looking down the droopy lid is higher (the opposite of acquired ptosis).
Can come with superior rectus weakness (they develop together).
Amblyopia usually comes from the refractive error, not the ptosis itself.
Operate in the preschool years, or earlier if the lid covers the pupil. Usually a levator resection.
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking (~5% of congenital ptosis): a branch of CN V (pterygoid) is wired to the levator. The lid lifts when chewing, sucking, or opening the mouth. Doesn't improve with age.
3rd nerve misdirection: odd lid lifts with certain eye movements (e.g. on looking down or across). Usually after an acquired 3rd nerve palsy.
Severe jaw-wink or misdirection → levator disinsertion + brow suspension.
chunks.hook: Baby lifts the lid while feeding → Marcus Gunn ('the gum-chewing wink').

cards.q: In downgaze, is a congenital ptotic lid higher or lower than the normal lid?
cards.a: Higher (lid lag: the levator doesn't relax).

cards.q: Which nerve is misdirected in Marcus Gunn jaw-winking?
cards.a: Mandibular branch of CN V (pterygoid) → levator.

chunks.title: Involutional ptosis & lid anatomy
chunks.tldr: Old-age ptosis = stretched levator aponeurosis: high crease, good levator function, worse at the end of the day.
points: Usually both sides. High lid crease, good levator function, deep upper sulcus, thin lid.
Gets worse in the evening (Müller fatigue) → can mimic myasthenia.
Aponeurosis joins the septum ~4 mm above the tarsus and inserts on the lower third of the front of the tarsus.
Asian lids: low or absent crease in ~50%, because the aponeurosis and septum insert lower.
Müller muscle attaches to the top edge of the tarsus. Lower-lid equivalents: capsulopalpebral fascia and the inferior tarsal muscle.
Mechanical ptosis: dermatochalasis, tumour (neurofibroma), scar, swelling.
chunks.hook: Old lid: muscle fine, tendon tired → high crease + good function.

cards.q: Elderly patient: ptosis worse in the evening, high crease, levator function 14 mm. Diagnosis?

chunks.title: Ptosis surgery: which operation?
chunks.tldr: Choose by levator function: ≥10 mm → Müller resection. ≥5 mm → levator advancement. <4 mm → brow suspension.
points: Conjunctiva–Müller resection: lifts only 2–3 mm. For mild ptosis with good levator (≥10 mm), e.g. Horner, mild congenital.
Levator advancement/resection: any cause, if levator function is ≥5 mm. Skin or conjunctival approach (posterior gives a more predictable contour).
Brow (frontalis) suspension: severe ptosis with poor levator (<4 mm), e.g. 3rd nerve palsy, BPES, failed resection. Sling made of fascia lata, Prolene or silicone.
Check the Bell phenomenon and tear film before surgery: a weak Bell → exposure keratopathy after surgery.
chunks.hook: Good muscle → tighten it. No muscle → borrow the brow.

cards.q: Horner ptosis 2 mm, levator 14 mm: best operation?
BPES with levator function 2 mm: which operation?

chunks.title: Involutional ectropion
chunks.tldr: Old lower lid falls outward because it's loose. Fix it with a lateral tarsal strip.
points: Causes watering (punctum turned away), red exposed conjunctiva, and later keratinised conjunctiva.
Snap test: pull the lid ≥8 mm from the globe. If it doesn't snap back without a blink → horizontal laxity.
Lateral canthal laxity: rounded lateral corner, lid pulls medially >2 mm.
Medial canthal laxity: pull the lid laterally. The punctum normally moves only 1–2 mm. Mild laxity: it reaches the limbus. Severe: it reaches the pupil.
Generalised ectropion → lateral tarsal strip (or pentagon excision).
Medial ectropion → medial spindle (diamond of conjunctiva) + tightening.
Bad medial canthal laxity → stabilise it first, or the punctum gets dragged laterally.
chunks.hook: Ectropion = lid goes Exit (out). Entropion = lid goes ENter (in).

cards.q: Standard operation for generalised involutional ectropion?
Lid pulled laterally: the punctum reaches the pupil. What does this mean?

chunks.title: Scar, paralytic & mechanical ectropion
chunks.tldr: Scar ectropion → push the skin up and it gets better → needs more skin. Facial palsy → protect the cornea first.
points: Cicatricial: scarred, short skin pulls the lid out (burns, trauma, dermatitis). Worse when opening the mouth. Fix with Z-plasty, flaps, or skin grafts (from upper lid, behind or in front of the ear, or above the collarbone).
Paralytic (CN VII palsy): lagophthalmos → exposure keratopathy, and watering (punctum out, tear pump fails).
Temporary: lubricants, tape at night, botox to the levator (makes a ptosis), temporary tarsorrhaphy (especially with a poor Bell).

Permanent (no recovery after 6–12 months, or nerve cut e.g. after acoustic neuroma surgery): medial canthoplasty, lateral sling/strip, platinum (or gold) weight in the upper lid, lateral tarsorrhaphy.
Mechanical: a tumour pushes the lid out → remove it.
chunks.hook: Facial palsy rule: Cornea first, cosmetics later.
pearls: Platinum is preferred over gold weights: thinner, better contour, fewer revisions.

cards.q: Ectropion that gets worse when the patient opens their mouth?
Upper lid implant for lagophthalmos in facial palsy?

chunks.title: Entropion
chunks.tldr: Old lower lid rolls inward: laxity + weak retractors + overriding orbicularis. Scar entropion = conjunctival scarring.
points: Lashes rub the cornea (pseudotrichiasis) → PEEs, pannus, ulcers.
Causes: horizontal laxity, retractor disinsertion (lid moves less on downgaze), preseptal orbicularis overriding the pretarsal part.
Quick fixes: lubricant, tape, bandage contact lens, botox.
Everting sutures: fast, last months, good for frail or confused patients.
Wies procedure: full-thickness split + everting sutures. Lasting.
Retractor reinsertion: the most direct fix. Add a lateral tarsal strip for laxity.
Cicatricial entropion: trachoma, OCP, SJS, chemicals. Mild → tarsal fracture. Severe → grafts.

cards.q: Quick entropion repair for a frail, confused patient?
Name 2 causes of cicatricial entropion.
cards.a: Trachoma, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (also SJS, chemical injury).

chunks.title: Floppy eyelid syndrome
chunks.tldr: Obese man, rubbery upper lid that flips inside out easily, chronic red eye → check for sleep apnoea.
points: Sleeps face-down on the pillow → lid pulls away → exposure at night.
Very loose upper lid with a rubbery tarsus. Everts with almost no effort.
Upper tarsal papillary conjunctivitis, punctate keratitis, filaments.
Strong link with obstructive sleep apnoea (heart and lung disease). FES + OSA → higher glaucoma risk.
Ask about snoring and daytime sleepiness → refer for a sleep study.
Treat: weight loss, OSA treatment, shield or tape at night. Severe → upper-lid pentagon resection ≥10 mm.
Eyelid imbrication: the upper lid overlaps the lower when closing, so lower lashes rub the upper lid. Often with FES.

cards.q: Systemic disease strongly linked with floppy eyelid syndrome?

chunks.title: Lid retraction, varix, blepharochalasis
chunks.tldr: Commonest cause of lid retraction = thyroid eye disease. Also look at the other eye for ptosis.
points: Retraction = upper lid at or above the upper limbus.

Causes: TED (number 1), ptosis on the other side (Hering), facial palsy, 3rd nerve misdirection, Marcus Gunn, Collier sign (Parinaud dorsal midbrain), setting-sun sign (hydrocephalus), Parkinson, sympathomimetic drops, liver disease (Summerskill), over-corrected ptosis surgery.
Treat: Müller recession (mild) or levator recession (moderate–severe).
Lower-lid retraction: after blepharoplasty, TED → retractor recession + spacer graft.
Varix: purple compressible lump that gets bigger with Valsalva. May connect to the orbit.
Blepharochalasis: teens, repeated episodes of painless lid swelling → thin 'cigarette-paper' skin, ptosis.

cards.q: Lid retraction + upgaze palsy + light-near dissociation?
cards.a: Collier sign in Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome.

cards.q: Lid lesion that swells with Valsalva?

chunks.title: Cosmetic lid surgery basics
chunks.tldr: Ageing = loose skin + fat bulging + sagging brow. Check for ptosis, brow ptosis and dry eye before blepharoplasty.
points: Botox: crow's feet, frown lines. Risks: temporary ptosis, diplopia, ectropion.
Fillers: hyaluronic acid (lasts 3–12 months), fat (permanent).
Upper blepharoplasty: removes extra skin ± fat. Too much skin removed → lagophthalmos. Too much fat → hollow sulcus.
Lower blepharoplasty: anterior approach (extra skin) or transconjunctival approach (fat only). Risks: retraction, ectropion.
Brow ptosis must be fixed before or with blepharoplasty (direct or endoscopic brow lift).
chunks.hook: Lift the brow before you cut the lid.

cards.q: Main risk of removing too much upper-lid skin?

chunks.title: Congenital lid shapes: folds, telecanthus, BPES
chunks.tldr: BPES = small fissures + ptosis + epicanthus inversus + telecanthus. FOXL2 gene. Type I = ovarian failure.
points: Epicanthic folds: can make a child look esotropic (pseudoesotropia).
Telecanthus: long medial canthal tendons → wide gap between the inner corners. Not the same as hypertelorism (wide bony orbits).
BPES: AD, FOXL2 on chromosome 3. Type I has premature ovarian failure, type II doesn't.
BPES: amblyopia in ~50%. Fix the folds and telecanthus first, then a frontalis sling.
Epiblepharon: extra skin fold pushes lashes up (common in East Asians). Pull the skin down → the lashes turn out normally. Often gets better on its own.
Congenital entropion: true inturning (retractor problem) → Hotz procedure.

cards.q: Gene in BPES?
How do you tell epiblepharon from congenital entropion?
cards.a: Pull the skin fold down: in epiblepharon the lashes go back to normal.

chunks.title: Colobomas & rare lid malformations
chunks.tldr: Upper-lid coloboma → Goldenhar. Lower-lid coloboma → Treacher Collins.
points: Upper lid coloboma: junction of middle and inner thirds. Linked to cryptophthalmos and Goldenhar.
Lower lid coloboma: junction of middle and outer thirds. Treacher Collins (jaw and ear problems, slanted fissures).
Cryptophthalmos: skin runs right over the eye with no lids. Fraser syndrome (syndactyly, urogenital problems).
Euryblepharon: fissure too wide → lateral ectropion, exposure.
Ablepharon: missing front lid layer. Ablepharon-macrostomia: big 'fish' mouth.
Congenital upper lid eversion: Down syndrome, collodion baby (ichthyosis).
Ankyloblepharon filiforme adnatum: thin bands join the lids → snip them.

cards.q: Lower lid coloboma at the lateral third + small jaw + ear anomalies?
Cryptophthalmos + syndactyly?
